questions.stem: What is the difference between the defer and async attributes on a <script> tag?

options.A: defer and async both block HTML parsing while the script downloads
options.B: async downloads the script in parallel and executes it immediately when downloaded — potentially before parsing is complete, in any order. defer downloads the script in parallel but executes it only after HTML parsing is complete, in document order — safe for DOM-dependent scripts
options.C: defer executes scripts before the <head> is parsed; async waits for the full page
options.D: Both are identical — they only affect mobile browsers

questions.explanation: No attribute: parser blocks on download AND execution. async: non-blocking download, executes as soon as downloaded (unpredictable order — avoid for interdependent scripts). defer: non-blocking download, executes after DOMContentLoaded in source order — the correct default for most scripts. Rule of thumb: <script defer src='app.js'> in <head> for all non-critical scripts. async only for fully independent scripts (analytics).
questions.source: MDN Web Docs. <script> — defer and async. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/script#attributes; Grigorik. High Performance Browser Networking. O'Reilly, 2013.

questions.stem: What does <link rel='preload'> do, and when should it be used?

options.A: preload caches the resource permanently in the browser across all future visits
options.B: preload instructs the browser to fetch a critical resource early in the page load — before it is discovered in the normal parsing flow — without blocking rendering. Used for above-the-fold images, web fonts, and critical scripts to reduce LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)
options.C: preload is identical to prefetch — both load resources for the next page
options.D: preload is deprecated and replaced by HTTP/2 Server Push

questions.explanation: <link rel='preload' as='font' href='font.woff2' type='font/woff2' crossorigin>. The as attribute is mandatory — tells the browser the resource type for correct priority and Content Security Policy checking. Use preload for: LCP hero image, critical web fonts (prevents FOUT), key JS bundles needed for first interaction. Misuse (preloading non-critical resources) degrades performance by competing with critical resources. Distinct from prefetch (low-priority, next-page resources).
questions.source: MDN Web Docs. Preloading content with rel=preload. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Attributes/rel/preload; web.dev. Preload critical assets. https://web.dev/preload-critical-assets

questions.stem: Why does specifying width and height attributes on elements improve Core Web Vitals performance?

options.A: width and height attributes make images load faster by compressing them
options.B: When width and height are specified, the browser can calculate the image's aspect ratio before the image downloads and reserve the correct space in the layout — preventing Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) as images load in and push content down
options.C: width and height are only needed for SVG images, not raster images
options.D: Specifying dimensions enables browser-side image compression

questions.explanation: CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) is a Core Web Vitals metric measuring unexpected layout movement. Without dimensions: browser allocates 0×0 space → image loads → layout shifts → CLS score increases. With width='800' height='600': browser calculates 4:3 aspect ratio, reserves space via intrinsic aspect-ratio. Modern CSS: img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } respects the declared ratio responsively. Google's CWV threshold: CLS < 0.1 for 'Good'.
questions.source: web.dev. Cumulative Layout Shift. https://web.dev/cls; MDN Web Docs. Images in HTML. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/HTML/Multimedia_and_embedding/Images_in_HTML

questions.stem: What is the srcset attribute on , and how does it improve performance on different screen densities and sizes?

options.A: srcset allows the browser to load multiple images simultaneously for faster display
options.B: srcset provides a list of image candidates at different resolutions or widths — the browser selects the most appropriate one based on device pixel ratio and viewport size, serving retina-quality images to HiDPI screens while serving smaller files to standard displays
options.C: srcset is a CSS property that replaces the src attribute on images
options.D: srcset is only supported in Chrome and not cross-browser compatible

questions.explanation: Width descriptor: srcset='img-400.jpg 400w, img-800.jpg 800w, img-1600.jpg 1600w' with sizes='(max-width: 600px) 400px, 800px'. Browser picks the best candidate. Pixel density descriptor: srcset='img.jpg 1x, img@2x.jpg 2x' — serve 2× image on Retina displays. Without srcset: mobile devices download full desktop images (~300KB+). With srcset: mobile may get a 40KB version. Critical for LCP and data-conscious users.
questions.source: MDN Web Docs. Responsive images. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/HTML/Multimedia_and_embedding/Responsive_images; web.dev. Serve responsive images. https://web.dev/serve-responsive-images

questions.stem: A page has a hero image (above the fold, 1200px wide on desktop, full-width on mobile) that is the LCP element. Write the optimal HTML to maximise LCP performance.
questions.explanation: Option B is optimal: srcset provides responsive image candidates; sizes tells browser which candidate to pick at each viewport width; alt is descriptive; width/height prevent CLS; fetchpriority='high' overrides the browser's default priority heuristic to load the LCP image sooner (replaces the older <link rel=preload> pattern). Crucially: NO loading='lazy' on above-the-fold LCP images — lazy loading delays the LCP element. Option C applies lazy loading to the LCP image — a critical performance anti-pattern.
questions.source: web.dev. Largest Contentful Paint. https://web.dev/lcp; MDN. fetchpriority. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLImageElement/fetchPriority

mini_quizzes.title: MQ-2 · HTML APIs and Web Components

questions.stem: What is the HTML <template> element and what is its key behaviour in the browser?

options.A: <template> defines a CSS template layout applied to child elements
options.B: <template> holds inert HTML markup that is parsed but not rendered or executed — its content is stored in a DocumentFragment and can be cloned and inserted into the DOM dynamically via JavaScript, making it the foundation of Web Components
options.C: <template> is a server-side element that renders HTML partials
options.D: <template> is identical to <div> but with a semantic name for layout sections

questions.explanation: <template> content: not rendered, scripts not executed, images not loaded, styles not applied — until JavaScript clones and appends it. const tmpl = document.querySelector('template'); const clone = tmpl.content.cloneNode(true); document.body.appendChild(clone). Used in Web Components to define shadow DOM structure. Critical distinction: content is in template.content (a DocumentFragment), not template itself.
questions.source: MDN Web Docs. <template>. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/template; MDN. Web Components. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_components

questions.stem: What are the three core technologies that make up Web Components?

options.A: React, Vue, and Angular
options.B: Custom Elements (define new HTML elements with custom behaviour), Shadow DOM (encapsulated DOM and CSS scoped to the component), and HTML Templates (<template> and <slot> for reusable markup)
options.C: Web Workers, Service Workers, and Web Sockets
options.D: CSS Grid, Flexbox, and CSS Variables

questions.explanation: Web Components: (1) Custom Elements — class MyComponent extends HTMLElement { connectedCallback(){} } + customElements.define('my-component', MyComponent). Use as <my-component>. (2) Shadow DOM — this.attachShadow({mode:'open'}) creates isolated DOM/CSS. Styles don't leak in or out. (3) HTML Templates — <template> defines the markup; <slot> defines insertion points for light DOM content (slot='header'). All are native browser APIs, no framework required.
questions.source: MDN Web Docs. Web Components. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_components; web.dev. Web Components. https://web.dev/web-components

questions.stem: What is Shadow DOM encapsulation and why is it valuable for component-based development?

options.A: Shadow DOM is a security feature that hides HTML source code from browser developer tools
options.B: Shadow DOM creates an isolated DOM subtree attached to an element where styles and scripts are scoped to the component — global CSS cannot affect the component's internals, and the component's styles cannot leak out — enabling truly reusable components without naming collision or style conflicts
options.C: Shadow DOM improves rendering performance by hiding off-screen components
options.D: Shadow DOM is only available in Chrome and Safari, not Firefox

questions.explanation: Shadow DOM solves CSS global scope problems: a button component's :hover styles won't accidentally affect other buttons on the page. Terminology: shadow host (the custom element), shadow root (the root of the shadow tree), shadow tree (internal DOM), light DOM (children passed by the consumer via <slot>). Mode 'open': JS outside can access shadowRoot. Mode 'closed': shadowRoot returns null externally. Used in browser-native elements: <input>, <video> controls use shadow DOM.
questions.source: MDN Web Docs. Using shadow DOM. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_components/Using_shadow_DOM

questions.stem: How does the <dialog> element compare to a custom div-based modal in terms of accessibility and built-in behaviour?

options.A: <dialog> and custom div modals are identical in accessibility and behaviour
options.B: <dialog> provides built-in: focus trapping (keyboard focus is constrained to the dialog while open), the ::backdrop pseudo-element for overlay, the showModal()/close() API, and correct ARIA role='dialog' semantics — all of which must be manually implemented for a div-based modal, where common errors cause keyboard navigation to escape the modal
options.C: Custom div modals are more accessible than <dialog> because they are more flexible
options.D: <dialog> is only supported in Firefox and not cross-browser compatible

questions.explanation: <dialog> native benefits: (1) focus trap — Tab key stays within dialog; (2) Escape key closes modal dialogs automatically; (3) ::backdrop for the semi-transparent overlay (no extra div); (4) role='dialog' and aria-modal semantics; (5) showModal() pushes to the top layer (above fixed positioning). Custom div modals commonly miss focus trapping, causing keyboard and screen reader users to navigate behind the modal. <dialog> is now baseline-supported (Chrome, Firefox, Safari 2022+).
questions.source: MDN Web Docs. <dialog>. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/dialog; web.dev. Building a dialog component. https://web.dev/building-a-dialog-component

questions.stem: Design a reusable <info-card> Web Component that displays a title and description passed as attributes. Outline the implementation.

options.A: Use a <div class='info-card'> with CSS — Web Components are not needed for simple UI
options.B: (1) Define class InfoCard extends HTMLElement; (2) attach shadow DOM in constructor with this.attachShadow({mode:'open'}); (3) in connectedCallback, read this.getAttribute('title') and this.getAttribute('description'); (4) set shadowRoot.innerHTML with a <template>-based structure including scoped <style>; (5) customElements.define('info-card', InfoCard); (6) use as <info-card title='Hello' description='World'></info-card>
options.C: Use document.createElement('div') with id='info-card' — custom element names require a hyphen which is a syntax error
options.D: Web Components require a build tool like Webpack — they cannot be written in plain HTML/JS

questions.explanation: Custom element names MUST contain a hyphen (info-card) — this distinguishes them from native HTML elements and prevents future naming conflicts. Implementation: constructor() calls super() first; attachShadow in constructor; connectedCallback fires when element is added to DOM; observedAttributes + attributeChangedCallback handle dynamic attribute updates. Shadow DOM scopes the <style> block. No build tools required — native browser APIs.
questions.source: MDN Web Docs. Using custom elements. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_components/Using_custom_elements

mini_quizzes.title: MQ-3 · Content Security, Integrity and Security Headers

questions.stem: What is Subresource Integrity (SRI) and why is it important when loading scripts or stylesheets from a CDN?

options.A: SRI compresses CSS and JS files served from CDNs to reduce file size
options.B: SRI uses a cryptographic hash in the integrity attribute on <script> and <link> elements — the browser verifies the downloaded file matches the hash before executing it, protecting against CDN compromise where an attacker replaces a legitimate library with malicious code
options.C: SRI is a server-side technique that encrypts CDN traffic using HTTPS
options.D: SRI prevents hotlinking of images from third-party CDNs

questions.explanation: SRI example: <script src='https://cdn.example.com/lib.js' integrity='sha384-abc123...' crossorigin='anonymous'></script>. If the CDN serves a file with a different hash (due to compromise or supply chain attack), the browser refuses to execute it. The crossorigin='anonymous' attribute is required for cross-origin SRI checks (sends CORS request without credentials). Generate hashes at: https://www.srihash.org or via openssl dgst -sha384 -binary file.js | openssl base64.
questions.source: MDN Web Docs. Subresource Integrity. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Subresource_Integrity; W3C. SRI Specification. https://www.w3.org/TR/SRI

questions.stem: What does the sandbox attribute on an <iframe> do?

options.A: sandbox makes the iframe load content faster by caching it locally
options.B: sandbox applies a strict set of restrictions to the iframe's content — blocking scripts, form submission, popups, and same-origin access by default. Specific capabilities can be selectively re-enabled using values like allow-scripts or allow-forms
options.C: sandbox prevents the iframe from displaying third-party cookies
options.D: sandbox forces the iframe content to load over HTTPS

questions.explanation: sandbox with no value: maximum restrictions — no scripts, no forms, no popups, no same-origin access, treated as unique origin. Selective re-enabling: sandbox='allow-scripts allow-same-origin'. Warning: allow-scripts + allow-same-origin together can allow the framed content to remove the sandbox attribute — use carefully. Best practice for untrusted content: sandbox='allow-scripts' only. Used for embedding user-generated content, third-party widgets, and online code editors.
questions.source: MDN Web Docs. <iframe> sandbox. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/iframe#sandbox; HTML Living Standard. https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/iframe-embed-object.html

questions.stem: What is a Content Security Policy (CSP) and how does the <meta http-equiv='Content-Security-Policy'> tag relate to HTTP header-based CSP?

options.A: CSP is an HTML attribute that prevents XSS by blocking all inline JavaScript
options.B: CSP is a security policy delivered via HTTP header (Content-Security-Policy) or <meta> tag that tells browsers which content sources are trusted — restricting script, style, image, and font origins to prevent XSS and data injection. The <meta> tag approach has limitations: it cannot use frame-ancestors, sandbox, or report-uri directives, making HTTP headers the preferred delivery method
options.C: CSP is only effective against CSRF attacks, not XSS
options.D: The <meta> CSP tag is identical to the HTTP header in all respects

questions.explanation: CSP example: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://cdn.trusted.com; img-src *; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'. Via meta: <meta http-equiv='Content-Security-Policy' content='default-src self'>. Meta CSP limitations: cannot set frame-ancestors (clickjacking protection), sandbox, or report-uri. HTTP header is processed before any HTML parsing — stronger protection. Strict CSP eliminates 'unsafe-inline' which blocks most XSS vectors.
questions.source: MDN Web Docs. Content Security Policy. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CSP; web.dev. Content Security Policy. https://web.dev/csp

questions.stem: What is Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and how does proper HTML escaping prevent it?

options.A: XSS is an attack where an attacker gains physical access to a web server
options.B: XSS: an attacker injects malicious scripts into web pages viewed by other users — typically by exploiting unescaped user input rendered as HTML. Prevention: escape all user-supplied data before inserting into HTML (& → &, < → <, > → >, ' → ', ' → ") — converting characters that have HTML meaning into harmless entities
options.C: XSS only affects websites that use JavaScript — static HTML sites are immune
options.D: HTML escaping is only needed for content inside <script> tags

questions.explanation: Reflected XSS: user input returned in the page without escaping. Stored XSS: malicious input persisted in DB then rendered. DOM XSS: client-side JavaScript writes user input to innerHTML. Prevention: (1) output encoding — escape before rendering in HTML context; (2) use textContent/innerText instead of innerHTML; (3) CSP blocks inline scripts even if injection succeeds; (4) sanitise HTML with DOMPurify when rich text is required. innerHTML with user data is a critical vulnerability.
questions.source: OWASP. Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet. https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html

questions.stem: A developer writes: document.getElementById('output').innerHTML = userInput; to display a user's name on the page. Evaluate the security risk and provide the correct fix.

options.A: No risk — innerHTML is the standard way to display user content
options.B: Critical DOM XSS vulnerability: if userInput contains or , the script executes in the user's browser with full page access. Fix: use textContent instead — document.getElementById('output').textContent = userInput — which treats the input as plain text and never executes it as HTML. If HTML formatting is required, sanitise with DOMPurify.sanitize(userInput) before assigning to innerHTML
options.C: The risk is low — browsers block script injection via innerHTML automatically
options.D: Fix by adding encodeURIComponent(userInput) before assigning to innerHTML

questions.explanation: innerHTML parses and executes HTML including event handlers: steals session cookies. textContent is the correct fix — it sets the text node content without parsing HTML. encodeURIComponent (option D) encodes for URLs, not HTML — does not prevent XSS in innerHTML context. DOMPurify is the correct sanitiser when rich HTML is genuinely required (user-submitted blog posts, comments).
questions.source: OWASP. DOM XSS. https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/DOM_Based_XSS; MDN Web Docs. Element.innerHTML — Security considerations. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/innerHTML#security_considerations

mini_quizzes.title: MQ-4 · HTML and SEO, Structured Data and Modern Patterns

questions.stem: What is JSON-LD structured data in HTML, and what is its purpose?

options.A: JSON-LD is a JavaScript library for loading data from REST APIs
options.B: JSON-LD (JSON for Linked Data) is a structured data format embedded in a <script type='application/ld+json'> block in HTML — it describes page content using Schema.org vocabulary, enabling search engines to understand entities (products, events, recipes, reviews) and display rich results (star ratings, prices, event dates) in SERPs
options.C: JSON-LD is a CSS-in-JS technique for styling components
options.D: JSON-LD is Google's proprietary format for AMP (Accelerated Mobile Pages)

questions.explanation: JSON-LD example: <script type='application/ld+json'>{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"Product","name":"Widget","offers":{"@type":"Offer","price":"9.99","priceCurrency":"GBP"}}</script>. Google, Bing, and Yahoo parse this to generate rich snippets. Preferred by Google over Microdata or RDFa because it does not require modifying existing HTML markup — cleanly separates structured data from presentation.
questions.source: Google. Introduction to structured data. https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/intro-structured-data; Schema.org. https://schema.org

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the <link rel='canonical'> element in HTML?

options.A: rel='canonical' loads the website's CSS stylesheet
options.B: rel='canonical' tells search engines which URL is the preferred (canonical) version of a page when the same content is accessible via multiple URLs — preventing duplicate content penalties in search rankings
options.C: rel='canonical' marks a page as the homepage of the website
options.D: rel='canonical' is used to specify the language of the page content

questions.explanation: Duplicate content scenarios: HTTP vs HTTPS, www vs non-www, URL parameters (?ref=email), paginated pages. Example: <link rel='canonical' href='https://www.example.com/product/widget'> on all variants. Without canonical tags, search engines may split PageRank across duplicate URLs or index the wrong version. Self-referential canonical (page points to itself) is best practice on all pages. Also used for syndicated content to credit the original source.
questions.source: Google Search Central. Consolidate duplicate URLs. https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls; MDN Web Docs. rel=canonical. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Attributes/rel

questions.stem: What is the Intersection Observer API and how is it used in HTML/JavaScript for performance optimisation?

options.A: Intersection Observer tracks mouse cursor position relative to elements
options.B: Intersection Observer is a browser API that asynchronously observes when a target element enters or exits the viewport — enabling lazy loading of images/iframes, infinite scroll, and scroll-triggered animations without expensive scroll event listeners that block the main thread
options.C: Intersection Observer is a CSS feature that applies styles when elements overlap
options.D: Intersection Observer requires a polyfill in all browsers including Chrome

questions.explanation: const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => { entries.forEach(e => { if(e.isIntersecting) { e.target.src = e.target.dataset.src; observer.unobserve(e.target); } }); }, { rootMargin: '200px' }); document.querySelectorAll('img[data-src]').forEach(img => observer.observe(img)). Advantages over scroll listeners: runs off main thread, batched, threshold-based. rootMargin: '200px' starts loading 200px before the image enters viewport — prevents visible loading gaps.
questions.source: MDN Web Docs. Intersection Observer API. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Intersection_Observer_API; web.dev. Lazy loading images. https://web.dev/lazy-loading-images

questions.stem: How does the HTML element differ from for responsive images, and when should each be used?

options.A: and are identical — use either interchangeably
options.B: lets the browser choose the best resolution/size candidate — the art direction remains the same. enables art direction: serving completely different images (cropped, composed differently) at different viewport sizes using conditions, plus format switching (WebP with JPEG fallback). Use srcset for resolution switching; use for art direction or format negotiation
options.C: is deprecated in HTML5; use exclusively
options.D: supports WebP; only supports JPEG and PNG

questions.explanation: Resolution switching (srcset): same image, different sizes — browser chooses. art direction: — mobile gets a portrait crop, desktop gets the wide landscape. also for format negotiation: . Always include as fallback.
questions.source: MDN Web Docs. Responsive images. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/HTML/Multimedia_and_embedding/Responsive_images

questions.stem: Audit this HTML head section and identify all performance, SEO, and security issues: <head><title>Home</title><script src='app.js'></script><link rel='stylesheet' href='style.css'><meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width'></head>

options.A: No issues — this is a well-optimised HTML head
options.B: Four issues: (1) <script src='app.js'> blocks HTML parsing — add defer attribute; (2) <meta name='viewport'> missing initial-scale=1 — add content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1'; (3) Missing <meta charset='UTF-8'> — character encoding must be declared within first 1024 bytes; (4) Title 'Home' is non-descriptive for SEO — should be meaningful (e.g., 'Company Name — Homepage'). Additionally: missing <meta name='description'>, no CSP, no canonical link
options.C: Only the missing charset meta tag is an issue
options.D: The script tag should be moved to the <body> — that is the only fix needed

questions.explanation: (1) Render-blocking script: parser stops at <script> until download+execution complete — defer fixes this. (2) initial-scale=1 omission: some browsers may apply their own zoom level. (3) Missing charset: the HTML5 spec requires charset within the first 1024 bytes — missing it risks mojibake on non-ASCII content (browser must sniff encoding). (4) 'Home' title: search engines use title as the primary SERP label — non-descriptive titles hurt CTR and SEO. Moving to <body> (option D) is a legacy pattern; defer in <head> is the modern standard.
questions.source: MDN Web Docs. What's in the head. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/HTML/Introduction_to_HTML/The_head_metadata_in_HTML; web.dev. Render-blocking resources. https://web.dev/render-blocking-resources
